title: Not All 'Magic' Mushrooms Are the Same
gist: RAND researchers Michelle Priest and Beau Kilmer warn that Amanita muscaria ('fly agaric'), used by an estimated 3.5 million American adults in 2025 versus 11 million for psilocybin, is legally unregulated in nearly every U.S. state, materially more toxic than psilocybin mushrooms, and increasingly sold in unregulated gummies and chocolates -- creating a policy blind spot as psychedelic decriminalization spreads.

themes.theme: Scale and legal status of Amanita muscaria use

insights.claim: A RAND report estimated that about 3.5 million American adults used Amanita muscaria in 2025, compared with 11 million who reported using psychoactive psilocybin mushrooms.
insights.speaker: Michelle Priest
insights.so_what: Quantifies a meaningfully sized (3.5M-user) unregulated psychoactive-substance market that is largely absent from current psychedelics policy debate, relevant to nutraceutical/wellness-product regulators and investors in the psychedelics space.
insights.quote: we estimated that about 3.5 million American adults used Amanita muscaria in 2025, compared with 11 million who reported using psychoactive psilocybin mushrooms.

insights.claim: Amanita muscaria is not illegal under the federal Controlled Substances Act, and as of writing only one U.S. state (Louisiana) prohibits it, despite a 2024 FDA assessment finding it unsafe to eat or add to food.
insights.speaker: Michelle Priest
insights.so_what: A clear regulatory gap: a substance the FDA itself has flagged as unsafe remains almost entirely unregulated at the state level, creating legal-risk and first-mover regulatory-arbitrage dynamics for producers/retailers.
insights.quote: Amanita muscaria is not illegal under the federal Controlled Substances Act. And only one state, Louisiana, prohibits it. A 2024 assessment by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (PDF) found that it is not safe to eat or add to food.

insights.claim: In contrast to Amanita muscaria's unregulated status, psilocybin remains illegal under federal law and unapproved by the FDA as medicine, even though three states have legalized supervised psilocybin use and more than 30 cities/counties have deprioritized enforcement of psychedelics offenses.
insights.speaker: Michelle Priest
insights.so_what: Highlights an inverted regulatory risk profile: the more thoroughly studied and clinically promising substance (psilocybin) is more tightly regulated than the more toxic, less-studied one (Amanita muscaria) -- a policy inconsistency ripe for reform or enforcement action.
insights.quote: In addition to three states legalizing supervised psilocybin use, more than 30 cities and counties have “deprioritized” the enforcement of certain offenses related to psychedelics, including psilocybin.

insights.claim: Unlike the vast majority of psilocybin-containing mushrooms, Amanita muscaria can be quite toxic if not properly prepared, with effects ranging from nausea and vomiting to severe cases of seizures, coma, and in extremely rare instances death.
insights.speaker: Michelle Priest
insights.so_what: Establishes a materially different risk/liability profile compared to psilocybin, relevant to product-liability exposure for any company marketing Amanita-derived consumer products.
insights.quote: Unlike the vast majority (PDF) of mushrooms containing psilocybin, Amanita muscaria can be quite toxic. If not properly prepared, effects can include nausea and vomiting, with more severe cases involving seizures, coma and, in extremely rare instances, death.

insights.claim: A 2026 CDC review identified 180 cases of severe illness across 34 states linked to eating mushroom-containing products, some of which contained compounds from both Amanita muscaria and psilocybin mushrooms mixed with other unregulated substances.
insights.speaker: Michelle Priest
insights.so_what: A hard, dated public-health incident count (180 cases/34 states, 2026) that regulators and litigators could cite as grounds for tightening rules on unregulated mushroom products.
insights.quote: A 2026 review from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention identified 180 cases of severe illness in 34 states associated with eating mushroom-containing products.

insights.claim: The main active compound in Amanita muscaria is muscimol, which acts on brain neurotransmitters and produces effects most commonly described as an alcohol-like intoxicated feeling, sleepiness with altered dreams, and relaxation; no clinical trials have confirmed anecdotal claims that it reduces substance use or anxiety.
insights.speaker: Michelle Priest
insights.so_what: Notes an evidence gap between consumer marketing claims (anxiety relief, substance-use reduction) and clinical validation -- relevant for scrutinizing wellness-product health claims under FTC/FDA advertising rules.
insights.quote: Others report that it can help reduce substance use or alleviate anxiety, but no clinical trials have confirmed these health claims.

themes.theme: Product landscape and consumer confusion risk

insights.claim: Amanita muscaria is sold in unregulated gummies, chocolates, and other consumer products, and is also used for microdosing, despite being unregulated and potentially mixed with other harmful, undisclosed substances.
insights.speaker: Michelle Priest
insights.so_what: Identifies an active, unregulated consumer-products category (Amanita gummies/chocolates) that a regulatory crackdown could disrupt -- relevant to any investor exposed to unregulated wellness/nootropic product retailers.
insights.quote: It is also sold in unregulated gummies, chocolates, and other products.

insights.claim: Because products advertising Amanita muscaria imagery or claims may or may not actually contain it, and may contain undisclosed mixes of other unregulated intoxicants, consumers face meaningful uncertainty about what they are actually purchasing.
insights.speaker: Michelle Priest
insights.so_what: A labeling/adulteration risk that mirrors past unregulated-supplement scandals (e.g., kratom, delta-8 THC) -- a precedent pattern investors can use to anticipate eventual regulatory crackdowns and litigation exposure.
insights.quote: These products may contain Amanita muscaria, or they may not. They may also contain a mix of other unregulated intoxicants that can be harmful.

insights.claim: The authors lay out a menu of regulatory options for Amanita muscaria: outright prohibition (difficult to enforce against foragers), allowing personal growth/possession while banning retail sales (the Colorado psilocybin model), or full regulation with decisions on child-proof packaging, product testing, marketing restrictions, and taxes.
insights.speaker: Michelle Priest
insights.so_what: A reusable three-tier regulatory framework (prohibition / possession-only / full regulated market) applicable across the broader psychedelics and novel-intoxicant policy landscape, useful for scenario-planning regulatory outcomes.
insights.quote: Jurisdictions could also allow adults to grow and possess Amanita muscaria but prohibit retail sales, as Colorado has done with psilocybin mushrooms and some other nature-based psychedelics.

insights.claim: Regardless of legal or regulatory changes, the authors argue public health agencies should proactively expand education campaigns highlighting Amanita muscaria's specific risks given its growing popularity and accessibility.
insights.speaker: Michelle Priest
insights.so_what: A low-cost, near-term policy lever (public education) that could precede or substitute for more contentious legislative action -- a signal to watch for state/local health department initiatives.
insights.quote: The popularity and accessibility of Amanita muscaria suggests public health agencies should step up education campaigns that highlight their specific risks.
